Saturday. Mridul came home from the district football trials without his kit bag; he'd left it on the bus. He walked straight to his room and pulled the blanket over his head. When his elder brother Sumit knocked, he said, "Go away." At dinner he wanted only the dal-chawal with ghee that Ma made when he was small, and he ate it in bed.
Monday. He stayed home. He watched old cartoons on the laptop and answered everything with "hmm". Ma sat on the edge of his bed and rubbed his back without asking a single question.
Thursday. Mridul came out for breakfast. "I missed the header in the second half," he told Sumit. "That's where I lost it." Sumit nodded. "Next trials are in March. Want to practise headers on Sunday?" Mridul shrugged, then nodded.

qa.q: What did Mridul want to eat on Saturday?
qa.a: Only the dal-chawal with ghee that Ma made when he was small.

qa.q: Why might Mridul want his childhood dal-chawal and old cartoons after the trials?
qa.a: The failure hurt, and those early comforts help him feel soothed and safe while he isn't ready to talk.

qa.q: Which choice of Ma's helped the retreat ease, and why?
qa.a: Rubbing his back without asking questions, which gave him warmth and time instead of pressure, so he could talk by Thursday.

qa.q: What was it like for Sumit when Mridul said 'Go away' on Saturday?
qa.a: Sumit may have felt shut out and worried, but waiting paid off when Mridul chose to talk about the missed header.

grounding: Over several days a teenager who failed football trials retreats to bed, cartoons and childhood food, and comes back out after warmth and time.

passage: Kashish, come, sit with your Sachin Dadu. You think you're the first one to hide under a quilt after a trial? When I was sixteen, in Jalandhar, I tried out for the state hockey team. I was sure I'd be picked. I wasn't. I came home, climbed into bed with my shoes still on, and didn't come out for three days except to eat. And what did I want to eat? Only the sooji halwa my Bebe made when I was five. I wouldn't talk to anyone. My father wanted to drag me out. Bebe said, "Let him be small for a few days." She brought halwa, sat with me, hummed old songs. On the fourth day I went to the ground and just watched. By the next season I was back on it. So eat your khichdi, beta. The trial will still be there next year.

qa.q: What did young Sachin want to eat after the hockey trials?
qa.a: Only the sooji halwa his Bebe made when he was five.

qa.q: Why did young Sachin climb into bed with his shoes still on?
qa.a: He was crushed after being sure he'd be picked, and retreating to bed and childhood food helped him feel soothed while the hurt was fresh.

qa.q: Whose choice helped young Sachin more, his father's or Bebe's, and why?
qa.a: Bebe's: letting him 'be small for a few days' with halwa and company helped him walk back to the ground on the fourth day.

qa.q: Why might Dadu be telling Kashish this story now?
qa.a: Kashish seems to be hiding under a quilt after a failed trial, and Dadu wants Kashish to know the retreat is normal and eases with time.

grounding: A grandfather tells a grandchild how, at sixteen, he retreated to bed and childhood food after failing a hockey trial until warmth and time eased it.

Devika had not made the district badminton squad, and now there was a power cut. The fan was dead, the flat was stuffy, and her board exams were six weeks away. She lay curled on the bed under her old cartoon-print sheet, the one she had refused to throw out at twelve.
"I don't want to talk," she said when her mother, Manjula, came in with a candle. "I don't want dinner. Only curd rice. The way you made it when I had fever."
Manjula made it by candlelight, with a little mango pickle on the side. She didn't mention exams or the squad. She sat on the floor by the bed and fanned Devika with a newspaper until her own arm ached.
Near midnight, Devika said, "I was so close, Amma."
"I know," Manjula said.

qa.q: What did Devika ask for instead of dinner?
qa.a: Only curd rice, the way her mother made it when she had fever.

qa.q: Why might Devika want the curd rice from her fever days?
qa.a: After missing the squad, she wants to be comforted like a small child, and that food brings back the feeling of being looked after.

qa.q: What choice did Manjula make despite the power cut, and why did it help?
qa.a: She made the curd rice by candlelight and fanned Devika without mentioning exams, giving warmth and time so Devika could finally say how close she had been.

qa.q: What is the evening like for Manjula?
qa.a: Hot and tiring, with exams worrying in the background, but she puts her own worries aside and sits with Devika until her arm aches.

grounding: During a power cut a teenager who missed the district squad curls up in bed asking only for childhood food, and her mother's quiet warmth lets her talk.

Zeenat got home from the state swimming trials with her hair still wet and her name not on the list. She walked past everyone in their Kurla flat without a word, pulled the curtain across her corner of the room, and got into bed in her tracksuit.
"Talk to me, jaan," said her Nani, Dilnaz. Nothing.
At dinner Zeenat wanted only one thing: the soft rice with dal and a spoon of ghee that Nani used to make when she was six and had a cold. She ate it in bed, facing the wall.
Nani didn't ask about the trials. She sat on the edge of the bed, humming an old song, pressing Zeenat's feet through the blanket.
The next evening the curtain was half open. Zeenat came out, sat beside Nani on the sofa, and said, "I was two seconds off."

qa.a: The soft rice with dal and a spoon of ghee that Nani used to make when she was six and had a cold.

qa.a: Nani is probably worried and a little helpless, but seems to trust that staying nearby will matter more than pushing.

"Mehak? Beta, come have dinner."
"Not hungry."
"You've been in bed since four. Did the basketball trial—"
"Mumma, please. Don't."
"Okay. Okay." A pause. "Sonali di made rajma."
"...Can I have sweet sevaiyan? Like when I was small?"
"Sevaiyan? Now?"
"Please."
From the kitchen, Sonali called, "I'll make it. Extra raisins, the way you liked in Class 2."
Later:
"Mehak, can I sit here?"
"...Okay. Don't talk about it."
"I won't. Budge up." Sonali slid under the blanket and put on their old favourite film on her phone.
Mehak laughed once, then cried quietly into the pillow. Sonali just stayed.
Next morning:
"Di? I missed three baskets in a row. That's what did it."
"Want to shoot a few at the park?"
"Maybe tomorrow."

passage: I'm Abhinav, and when I didn't make the state under-seventeen cricket team, I went to bed and basically stayed there for three days. I wouldn't talk to anyone. When Mum asked what I wanted to eat, I said, "Curd rice. Like you made when I was small." That was all I ate: curd rice with a bit of pickle, in the steel bowl with the elephant on it. My friend Lalremsiami came over and sat on the floor by my bed, and I pulled the blanket over my head. She didn't leave. She just told me about her day. Mum kept bringing curd rice. Nobody told me to get up. On the fourth morning, I walked out to the balcony and looked at the ground where I used to practise. It didn't feel so impossible anymore.

qa.q: Why did Abhinav want only the curd rice from childhood?
qa.a: Abhinav felt crushed and ashamed after missing the team, and the childhood food was soothing, like being looked after when small.

qa.q: What helped Abhinav come out of the retreat?
qa.a: Warmth and time: Mum kept bringing curd rice without pushing, and Lalremsiami stayed and talked, until Abhinav was ready to get up.

qa.a: Lalremsiami might have felt worried but patient, choosing to stay and chat rather than force a conversation.

Note from Neelam, Madhav's mother, to his badminton coach.
Madhav came home from the district trials on Saturday and went straight to bed. He hasn't come out much since. He won't talk about the trials. When I ask what he wants to eat, it's only the moong dal khichdi I made when he was little, with ghee, in his old blue plate. He's fifteen, but he has his childhood blanket back on his bed. I haven't pushed. I sit with him a little each evening and don't ask questions. Yesterday he let me stroke his hair. I wanted you to know why he hasn't come to practice. I think he'll come back. He just needs some warmth and some days. If you could send him a short, kind message, I think it would help.

Diary, Tuesday. Yusuf.

Third day in bed. I didn't get into the district football squad. Coach read out the names and mine wasn't there.

I haven't really talked to anyone. Ammi keeps asking if I want anything, and all I want is her sevaiyan, the sweet one she used to make every Sunday when I was eight. She's made it three times now. She doesn't even ask why.

Kavitha didi came over today with a pile of my old comics. She didn't say anything about football. She just left them on my bed and sat and read one herself, laughing at the silly bits.

After she left I read two. I laughed at the one with the flying goat.

I think I might go outside tomorrow. Just to the gate.

She wouldn't talk to Aai. She wouldn't answer Seema tai. She only asked, in a small voice, for varan-bhaat with ghee the way Aai made it when she was little, and ate it in bed with a spoon.

Marek came back from the academy trial in Kraków on Sunday, dropped his skates by the door and went straight to bed. The coach's email had been short: not selected this year.

For two days he didn't answer anyone. He wouldn't come to dinner, but asked his father, Ivan, for the pancakes with jam he used to eat after swimming lessons when he was small. He watched old cartoons on his tablet with the blanket pulled up to his nose.

Ivan didn't push. He made the pancakes, left them on a tray, and sat on the floor by the bed with the newspaper, saying nothing much. On Wednesday Marek sat up and said, "I was too slow on the turns."

"Then we'll work on turns," Ivan said. "After you eat."
